entries.7d7ed90dcdb7fc0a791934b1ff0a755b5f401847: <div sID="gen11170" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="43" osisID="Ps.43" sID="Ps.43"/> <div eID="gen11170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11171" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11172" type="x-p"/> This psalm, it is likely, was penned upon the same occasion with the former, and, having no title, may be looked upon as an appendix to it; the malady presently returning, he had immediate recourse to the same remedy, because he had entered it in his book, with a "probatum est—it has been proved," upon it. The <reference osisRef="Ps.43.2-Ps.42.9">second verse</reference> of this psalm is almost the very same with the <reference osisRef="Ps.43.2-Ps.42.9">ninth verse</reference> of the foregoing psalm, as the <reference osisRef="Ps.43.5-Ps.42.11">fifth</reference> of this is exactly the same with the <reference osisRef="Ps.43.5-Ps.42.11">eleventh</reference> of that. Christ himself, who had the Spirit without measure, when there was occasion prayed a second and third time "saying the same words," <reference osisRef="Matt.26.44">Matt. xxvi. 44</reference>. In this psalm. I. David appeals to God concerning the injuries that were done him by his enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.43.1-Ps.43.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He prays to God to restore to him the free enjoyment of public ordinances again, and promises to make a good improvement of them, <reference osisRef="Ps.43.3-Ps.43.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. He endeavours to still the tumult of his own spirit with a lively hope and confidence in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.43.5">ver. 5</reference>), and if, in singing this psalm, we labour after these, we sing with grace in our hearts.
entries.59473949bfa32a68ebb53f0c629a4ac493b3037d: <div eID="gen11172" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11171" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Appeals and Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen11173" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man. 2 For thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the God of my strength: why dost thou cast me off? why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy? <hi type="super">3</hi> O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles. 4 Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God. 5 Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, <hi type="italic">who is</hi> the health of my countenance, and my God. <div eID="gen11173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11174" type="x-p"/> David here makes application to God, by faith and prayer, as his judge, his strength, his guide, his joy, his hope, with suitable affections and expressions. <div eID="gen11174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11175" type="x-p"/> I. As his Judge, his righteous Judge, who he knew would judge him, and who (being conscious of his own integrity) he knew would judge for him (<reference osisRef="Ps.43.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Judge me, O God! and plead my cause.</hi> There were those that impeached him; against them he is defendant, and from their courts, where he stood unjustly convicted and condemned, he appeals to the court of heaven, the supreme judicature, praying to have their judgment given against him reversed and his innocency cleared. There were those that had injured him; against them he is plaintiff, and exhibits his complaint to him who is the avenger of wrong, praying for justice for himself and upon them. Observe, 1. Who his enemies were with whom he had this struggle. Here was a sinful body of men, whom he calls an <hi type="italic">ungodly</hi> or <hi type="italic">unmerciful nation.</hi> Those that are unmerciful make it appear that they are ungodly; for, those that have any fear or love of their master will have compassion on their fellow-servants. And here was one bad man the head of them, a deceitful and unjust man, most probably Saul, who not only showed no kindness to David, but dealt most perfidiously and dishonestly with him. If Absalom was the man he meant, his character was no better. As long as there are such bad men out of hell, and nations of them, it is not strange that good men, who are yet out of heaven, meet with hard and base treatment. Some think that David, by the spirit of prophecy, calculated this psalm for the use of the Jews in their captivity in Babylon, and that the Chaldeans are the ungodly nation here meant; to them it was very applicable, but only as other similar scriptures, none of which are of private interpretation. God might design it for their use, whether David did or no. 2. What is his prayer with reference to them: <hi type="italic">Judge me.</hi> As to the quarrel God had with him for sin, he prays, "<hi type="italic">Enter not into judgment with me,</hi> for then I shall be condemned;" but, as to the quarrel his enemies had with him he prays, "Lord, <hi type="italic">judge me,</hi> for I know that I shall be justified; <hi type="italic">plead my cause against them,</hi> take my part, and in thy providence appear on my behalf." He that has an honest cause may expect that God will plead it. "Plead my cause so as to deliver me from them, that they may not have their will against me." We must reckon our cause sufficiently pleaded if we be delivered, though our enemies be not destroyed. <div eID="gen11175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11176" type="x-p"/> II. As his strength, his all-sufficient strength; so he eyes God (<reference osisRef="Ps.43.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou art the God of my strength, my God, my strength,</hi> from whom all my strength is derived, in whom I strengthen myself, who hast often strengthened me, and without whom I am weak as water and utterly unable either to do or suffer any thing for thee." David now went mourning, destitute of spiritual joys, yet he found God to be the God of his strength. If we cannot comfort ourselves in God, we may stay ourselves upon him, and may have spiritual supports when we want spiritual delights. David here pleads this with God: "Thou art the God on whom I depend as my strength; why then dost thou cast me off?" This was a mistake; for God never cast off any that trusted in him, whatever melancholy apprehensions they may have had of their own state. "Thou art the God of my strength; why then is my enemy too strong for me, and why go I mourning because of his oppressive power?" It is hard to reconcile the mighty force of the church's enemies with the almighty power of the church's God; but the day will reconcile them when all his enemies shall become his footstool. <div eID="gen11176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11177" type="x-p"/> III. As his guide, his faithful guide (<reference osisRef="Ps.43.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lead me, bring me to thy holy hill.</hi> He prays, 1. That God by his providence would bring him back from his banishment, and open a way for him again to the free enjoyment of the privileges of God's sanctuary. His heart is upon <hi type="italic">the holy hill and the tabernacles,</hi> not upon his family-comforts, his court-preferments, or his diversions; he could bear the want of these, but he is impatient to see God's tabernacles again; nothing so amiable in his eyes as those; thither he would gladly be brought back. In order to this he prays, "<hi type="italic">Send out thy light and thy truth;</hi> let me have this as a fruit of thy favour, which is light, and the performance of thy promise, which is truth." We need desire no more to make us happy than the good that flows from God's favour and is included in his promise. That mercy, that truth, is enough, is all; and, when we see these in God's providences, we see ourselves under a very safe conduct. Note, Those whom God leads he leads to his holy hill, and to his tabernacles; those therefore who pretend to be led by the Spirit, and yet turn their backs upon instituted ordinances, certainly deceive themselves. 2. That God by his grace would bring him into communion with himself, and prepare him for the vision and fruition of himself in the other world. Some of the Jewish writers by the <hi type="italic">light</hi> and <hi type="italic">truth</hi> here understand Messiah the Prince and Elias his forerunner: these have come, in answer to the prayers of the Old Testament; but we are still to pray for God's light and truth, the Spirit of light and truth, who supplies the want of Christ's bodily presence, to lead us into the mystery of godliness and to guide us in the way to heaven. When God sends his light and truth into our hearts, these will guide us to the upper world in all our devotions as well as in all our aims and expectations; and, if we conscientiously follow that light and that truth, they will certainly bring us to the holy hill above. <div eID="gen11177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11178" type="x-p"/> IV. As his joy, his exceeding joy. If God guide him to his tabernacles, if he restore him to his former liberties, he knows very well what he has to do: <hi type="italic">Then will I go unto the altar of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4">v. 4</reference>. He will get as near as he can unto God, his exceeding joy. Note, 1. Those that come to the tabernacles should come to the altar; those that come to ordinances should qualify themselves to come, and then come to special ordinances, to those that are most affecting and most binding. The nearer we come, the closer we cleave, to God, the better. 2. Those that come to the altar of God must see to it that therein they come unto God, and draw near to him with the heart, with a true heart: we come in vain to holy ordinances if we do not in them come to the holy God. 3. Those that come unto God must come to him as their exceeding joy, not only as their future bliss, but as their present joy, and that not a common, but an exceeding joy, far exceeding all the joys of sense and time. The phrase, in the original, is very emphatic—<hi type="italic">unto God the gladness of my joy,</hi> or of my triumph. Whatever we rejoice or triumph in God must be the joy of it; all our joy in it must terminate in him, and must pass through the gift to the giver. 4. When we come to God as our exceeding joy our comforts in him must be the matter of our praises to him as God, and our God: <hi type="italic">Upon the harp will I praise thee, O God! my God.</hi> David excelled at the harp (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.16">1 Sam. xvi. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.18">18</reference>), and with that in which he excelled he would praise God; for God is to be praised with the best we have; it is fit he should be, for he is the best. <div eID="gen11178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11179" type="x-p"/> V. As his hope, his never-failing hope, <reference osisRef="Ps.43.5">v. 5</reference>. Here, as before, David quarrels with himself for his dejections and despondencies, and owns he did ill to yield to them, and that he had no reason to do so: <hi type="italic">Why art thou cast down, O my soul?</hi> He then quiets himself in the believing expectation he had of giving glory to God (<hi type="italic">Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him</hi>) and of enjoying glory with God: <hi type="italic">He is the health of my countenance and my God.</hi> That is what we cannot too much insist upon, for it is what we must live and die by.  <chapter eID="Ps.43"/> <div eID="gen11179" type="x-p"/>

entries.f1cb2607781957f25b424767b80e7b2c00939228: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5962"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 43</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.43.1-Ps.43.5">Psa 43:1-5</reference>. Excepting the recurrence of the refrain, there is no good reason to suppose this a part of the preceding, though the scope is the same. It has always been placed separate.</title> <div sID="gen9075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5962"/><hi type="bold">1. Judge--</hi>or, "vindicate" (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.18">Psa 10:18</reference>).<div eID="gen9075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plead, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.35.1">Psa 35:1</reference>).<div eID="gen9076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ungodly--</hi>neither in character or condition objects of God's favor (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>). <div eID="gen9077" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3ac16503ebc5003ab5b653e091f10cd8c8d42c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5963"/><div sID="gen9078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5963"/><hi type="bold">2. God of my strength--</hi>by covenant relation my stronghold (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.1">Psa 18:1</reference>).<div eID="gen9078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast me off--</hi>in scorn.<div eID="gen9079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9080" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because--</hi>or, "in," that is, in such circumstances of oppression. <div eID="gen9080" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe6062a3eec7ff1a01a0741480f0e4be963e3883: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5964"/><div sID="gen9081" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5964"/><hi type="bold">3. light--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Psa 27:1</reference>.<div eID="gen9081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">truth--</hi>or, "faithfulness" (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference>), manifest it by fulfilling promises. Light and truth are personified as messengers who will bring him to the privileged place of worship.<div eID="gen9082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tabernacles--</hi>plural, in allusion to the various courts. <div eID="gen9083" type="x-p"/>
entries.8304c9addac819ef74aac116a074183ee50bb35c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5965"/><div sID="gen9084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5965"/><hi type="bold">4. the altar--</hi>as the chief place of worship. The mention of the harp suggests the prominence of praise in his offering. <chapter eID="Ps.43"/>

entries.585c5af6c99905c94254aa19fe4b41fa03f94c92: <div eID="gen20015" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20016" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20017" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20017" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20016" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20018" type="x-p"/> The psalmist begs God to take his part against his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.43.1">Psa 43:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.43.2">Psa 43:2</reference>; to send his light and truth to guide him to the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Psa.43.3">Psa 43:3</reference>; promises, if brought thither, to be faithful in the Divine service, <reference osisRef="Psa.43.4">Psa 43:4</reference>; chides himself for despondency, and takes courage, <reference osisRef="Psa.43.5">Psa 43:5</reference>. <div eID="gen20018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20019" type="x-p"/> There is no title to this Psalm in the Hebrew, nor in the Chaldee. The Syriac says it was composed "by David when Jonathan told him that Saul intended to slay him." The Arabic says of this, as of the preceding, that it is a prayer for the backsliding Jews. It is most evidently on the same subject with the forty-second Psalm, had the same author or authors, and contains the remaining part of the complaint of the captive Jews in Babylon. It is written as a part of the forty-second Psalm in forty-six of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. <div eID="gen20019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20020" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20021" type="x-p"/> Judge me, O God, and plead my cause - ריבה ריבי ribah ribi, a forensic term, properly enough translated, plead my cause, be my counsellor and advocate. <div eID="gen20021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20022" type="x-p"/> Ungodly nation - The Babylonians; the impious, perfidious, wicked, and deceitful Babylonians. <div eID="gen20022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20023" type="x-p"/> The deceitful and unjust man - Nebuchadnezzar.
entries.4c8744645d1ce59b62e4bbbc9af0e7458a5f4311: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20024" type="x-p"/> For those art the God of my strength - The psalmist speaks here, as in other places in the person of the whole Israelitish people then captive in Babylon. We still acknowledge thee for our God. Why are we cast off? Now that we are humbled and penitent, why are we not enlarged? Why are we not saved from this oppression of the Babylonians?
entries.f2f97131475fad1f365460e0d17ae584e41d41a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20025" type="x-p"/> O send out thy light and thy truth - We are in darkness and distress, O send light and prosperity; we look for the fulfillment of thy promises, O send forth thy truth. Let thy fight guide me to thy holy hill, to the country of my fathers; let thy truth lead me to thy tabernacles, there to worship thee in spirit and in truth.
entries.1a20fbc8afa554d2ee022f46eb371596ac206f96: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20026" type="x-p"/> Then will I go unto the altar - When thy light - a favorable turn on our affairs, leads us to the land of our fathers, and thy truth - the fulfillment of thy gracious promises, has placed us again at the door of thy tabernacles, then will we go to thy altar and joyfully offer those sacrifices and offerings which thy law requires, and rejoice in thee with exceeding great joy.
entries.89715ea235467367f0cfa48621787f3ef5a187cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20027" type="x-p"/> Why art thou cast down - Though our deliverance be delayed, God has not forgotten to be gracious. The vision, the prophetic declaration relative to our captivity, was for an appointed time. Though it appear to tarry, we must wait for it. In the end it will come, and will not tarry; why then should we be discouraged? Let us still continue to trust in God, for we shall yet praise him for the fullest proofs of his approbation in a great outpouring of his benedictions.  <chapter eID="Ps.43"/> <div eID="gen20027" type="x-p"/>

entries.c8d4c4d552362a4a79d8ae0235cf06a2b5de8c73: <reference osisRef="Ps.43.1-Ps.43.3">Psa 43:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9464" type="x-p"/> The Elohimic <hi type="italic">Judica</hi> (the introit of the so-called Cross or Passion Sunday which opens the <hi type="italic">celebritas Passionis</hi>), with which the supplicatory and plaintive first strophe of the Psalm begins, calls to mind the Jehovic <hi type="italic">Judica</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.9">Psa 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1">Psa 26:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.1">Psa 35:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.24">Psa 35:24</reference> : judge me, i.e., decide my cause (lxx κρῖνόν με, Symmachus κρῖνόν μοι). ריבה has the tone upon the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> before the ריבי which begins with the half-guttural ר, as is also the case in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.22">Psa 74:22</reference>; Psa 119:154. The second prayer runs: <hi type="italic">vindica me a gente impia</hi>; מן standing for <hi type="italic">contra</hi> in consequence of a <hi type="italic">constr. praegnans</hi>. לא־חסיד is here equivalent to one practising no חסד towards men, that is to say, one totally wanting in that חסד, by which God’s חסד is to be imitated and repaid by man in his conduct towards his fellow-men. There is some uncertainty whether by אישׁ one chief enemy, the leader of all the rest, is intended to be mentioned side by side with the unloving nation, or whether the special manner of his enemies is thus merely individualised. עולה means roguish, mischievous conduct, utterly devoid of all sense of right. In <reference osisRef="Ps.43.2">Psa 43:2</reference> the poet establishes his petition by a twofold Why. He loves God and longs after Him, but in the mirror of his present condition he seems to himself like one cast off by Him. This contradiction between his own consciousness and the inference which he is obliged to draw from his afflicted state cannot remain unsolved. אלהי מעזּי, God of my fortress, is equivalent to who is my fortress. Instead of אלך we here have the form אתהלּך, of the slow deliberate gait of one who is lost in his own thoughts and feelings. The sting of his pain is his distance from the sanctuary of his God. In connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.43.3">Psa 43:3</reference> one is reminded of <reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Psa 57:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.15.13">Exo 15:13</reference>, quite as much as of Psa 42:9. “Light and truth” is equivalent to mercy and truth. What is intended is the light of mercy or loving-kindness which is coupled with the truth of fidelity to the promises; the light, in which the will or purpose of love, which is God’s most especial nature, becomes outwardly manifest. The poet wishes to be guided by these two angels of God; he desires that he may be brought (according tot he <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> of the Babylonian text יבואוני, “let come upon me;” but the אל which follows does not suit this form) to the place where his God dwells and reveals Himself. “Tabernacles” is, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.84.2">Psa 84:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.46.5">Psa 46:5</reference>, an amplificative designation of the tent, magnificent in itself and raised to special honour by Him who dwells therein.
entries.9828cf3e4d86d233342af44720d7e27765c29c84: <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4-Ps.43.5">Psa 43:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen9464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9465" type="x-p"/> The poet, in anticipation, revels in the thought of that which he has prayed for, and calls upon his timorous soul to hope confidently for it. The cohortatives in <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4">Psa 43:4</reference> are, as in Ps 39:14 and frequently, an apodosis to the petition. The poet knows no joy like that which proceeds from God, and the joy which proceeds from Him he accounts as the very highest; hence he calls God אל שׂמחת גּילי, and therefore he knows no higher aim for his longing than again to be where the fountainhead of this exultant joy is (Hos 9:5), and where it flows forth in streams (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.9">Psa 36:9</reference>). Removed back thither, he will give thanks to Him with the cithern (<hi type="italic">Beth instrum</hi>.). He calls Him אלהים אלהי, an expression which, in the Elohim-Psalms, is equivalent to יהוה אלהי in the Jahve-Psalms. The hope expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4">Psa 43:4</reference> casts its rays into the prayer in Psa 43:3. In <reference osisRef="Ps.43.5">Psa 43:5</reference>, the spirit having taken courage in God, holds this picture drawn by hope before the distressed soul, that she may therewith comfort herself. Instead of wthmy, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.6">Psa 42:6</reference>, the expression here used, as in Ps 42:12, is וּמה־תּהמי. Variations like these are not opposed to a unity of authorship.  <chapter eID="Ps.43"/> <div eID="gen9465" type="x-p"/>

entries.2bffb6657cfa70acebd5525008c961f081697c8b:
PSALM 43
This psalm is very similar to the preceding.
This and the preceding psalm have been considered by the greater number of critics as having originally formed only one psalm, and they make but one in forty-six MSS. The similarity of the style, sentiment, and metrical structure, and the occurrence of the intercalary verse at verses 5th and 10th of Psalm 42, and verse 5th of Psalm 43, confirm this opinion. “The fact, indeed,” says Williams, “is self evident, and easily accounted for. The Jewish choristers having, on some occasion, found the anthem too long, have divided it for their own conveniency, (no uncommon thing among choristers,) and, being once divided, it was ignorantly supposed it ought to be so divided.”
David, who probably was the author of it, being chased and driven out of his country by the unjust violence and tyranny of his enemies, calls upon God for vengeance, and encourages himself to hope for restoration.
Psalm 43:1-5
1. Judge me, O God! and plead my cause: deliver me from the cruel [or unmerciful] nation, free me from the deceitful and wicked man. 2. For thou art the God of my strength; why art thou estranged from me? why go I sad because of the oppression of the enemy? 3. Send forth thy light and thy truth, let them direct me, let them conduct me to thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles. 4. And I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy, [literally the joy of my rejoicing:] and I will praise thee upon the harp, O God! my God. 5. O my soul! why art thou cast down? and why art thou disquieted within me? for I will yet praise him who is the help of my countenance, and my God.
 
1 Judge me, O God! David, in the first place, complains of the extreme cruelty of his enemies; but in the verses which immediately follow, he shows that there was nothing which he felt to be more grievous, than to be deprived of the opportunity of access to the sanctuary. We have an evidence of his enjoying the testimony of a good conscience in this, that he commends the defense of his cause to God. The term judge, which he first makes use of, is nothing else than to undertake the defense of one’s cause; and he expresses his meaning more clearly by adding, plead my cause The substance and object of his prayer, indeed, were, that he might be delivered from the wicked and malicious men by whom he was undeservedly persecuted. But as it is to the miserable and guiltless, who are wrongfully afflicted, that God promises his help, David, in the first place, submits himself to be examined by him, that, having discovered and thoroughly proved the rectitude of his cause, he may at length grant him aid. And as it is a most cheering source of consolation for us to find that God disdains not to take cognisance of our cause, so also, it is vain for us to expect that he will avenge the injuries and wrongs which are done to us, unless our own integrity be so manifest as to induce him to be favorable to us against our adversaries. By the unmerciful nation is to be understood the whole company of David’s enemies, who were cruel, and destitute of all the feelings of humanity. What follows, concerning the deceitful and wicked man, might indeed be applied to Saul; but it seems rather to be a form of speech in which, by enallage, the singular number is used for the plural.

entries.a3859b97232093e6f226dd6e18ab33d7d0b67283:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="43" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. XLIII.</ns0:head>

                     <ns0:head>The ARGUMENT.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p>This <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> seems to have been Composed by the same Author, and upon the same Occasion, with the former.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. JUdge me <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>Iudge,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>give Sentence</ns0:hi> for me, as this Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 26. 1. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>, O God, and plead my cause a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst an <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">

                     </ns0:note> nation <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">So he calls the Compa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny of his Enemies for their great Numbers, and because they were the far greatest part, and almost the whole Body, of the Nation.</ns0:note>: O deliver me <ns0:note place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>from a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                     </ns0:note> from the deceitful and unjust <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Who covereth his wicked Designs, with fair and false Pretences: Which sort of men are hateful to thee, and to all good Men.</ns0:note> man <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either <ns0:hi>Saul:</ns0:hi> Or rather, <ns0:hi>Achi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tophel,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Absalom.</ns0:hi> For he speaks of <ns0:hi>the holy Hill</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Zion,</ns0:hi> v. 3. which was not so till after <ns0:hi>Saul's</ns0:hi> time. Or, <ns0:hi>Man</ns0:hi> may be put Collectively, for the Men of that time.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. For thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> the God of my strength, why dost thou cast me off? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap>

                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 9.</ns0:note> Why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. O send out <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Actually impart and discover them: for at pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent thou seemest to Conceal and with-hold them from me. (<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Thy Favour, or the Light of thy Countenance, and the Truth of thy Promises made to me, as God's <ns0:hi>Mercy</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Truth</ns0:hi> oft go together, as, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 15. 20. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 61. 7. and 89. 14. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Or this may be a Figure called <ns0:hi>Hendiaduo,</ns0:hi> whereby <ns0:hi>Light and Truth</ns0:hi> is put either for <ns0:hi>the Light of Gods Truth;</ns0:hi> Or rather, for <ns0:hi>true Light,</ns0:hi> the Illumination of Gods Spirit, and the direction of his gracious Providence, whereby he might be led (as it follows) in the right way, which would bring him to God's holy Hill.</ns0:note> thy light and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 57. 3<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> thy truth <ns0:hi>g;</ns0:hi> let them lead me, let them bring me unto thy holy hill <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To wit, of <ns0:hi>Zion,</ns0:hi> the place of God's Presence and Worship.</ns0:note>, and to thy tabernacles <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Tabernacle. Which he calls <ns0:hi>Tabernacles,</ns0:hi> Either, 1. Because there were now two Tabernacles, one at <ns0:hi>Zion,</ns0:hi> where the Ark was; and another at <ns0:hi>Gibeon,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 16. 37. 39. Although he here seems to speak but of one of them, even of that which was upon God's holy Hill. Or, 2. Because of the several parts of it, the most Holy, and the Holy place, and the Church. These in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed were in that of <ns0:hi>Gibeon,</ns0:hi> but not in that of <ns0:hi>Zion.</ns0:hi> Or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 3. By a meer Enal<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>age of the Number, the plural for the singular; which is frequent as in other Words, so in those which belong to this Matter, as <ns0:hi>Tabernacles, Psal.</ns0:hi> 46. 4. and <ns0:hi>Sanctuaries, Levit.</ns0:hi> 26. 31. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 73. 17. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and 74. 7. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 51. 51. Nay the most Holy place, though but one simple part is by the Greeks called <ns0:hi>Holies.</ns0:hi> So in other Authors, we Read <ns0:hi>the Rivers of Nilus,</ns0:hi> of that one River, and <ns0:hi>Right hands,</ns0:hi> for one Right hand, and many like Phrases.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. Then will I go unto the altar of God <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To offer Sacrifices of Thanksgiving for my Deliverance.</ns0:note>, unto God <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the glad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of my joy.</ns0:note> my exceeding joy <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The principal Author and Matter of all my Joy and Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fort.</ns0:note>: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God, my God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 42. 5. 11.</ns0:note> Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, <ns0:hi>who is</ns0:hi> the health of my Countenance, and my God.</ns0:p>
